events.title: The Senior Man
events.body: The dean of your deanery has gone to the priests' residence with his knees and his photographs, and the bishop, who appoints deans and consults nobody, has asked {@vicar_for_clergy} to sound you out. That is how you learn that the chancery now counts you the senior man. It is not a promotion. A dean convenes the deanery meeting, signs the registers of parishes that have no pastor, sits on the presbyteral council by right, and drives to the chancery on the first Wednesday of the month to hear what the other deans have heard. It is four hours a week that {parish} will not get, and a title that brother priests treat as a rumor about you. The vicar for clergy would like an answer by Friday. He adds, as if it were a courtesy, that the bishop had also thought of {@brother_priest}, who is fifteen years younger, has a parish that runs itself, and has been asking, quietly, for something. You could take it. You could say the younger man should have it and mean it. You could take it and hand him the parts of it that teach.
events.flavorPrompt: A senior pastor offered the deanery: an honor that costs hours, and a younger priest who wants it.

choices.label: Accept. The deanery should be run by the man who has seen it longest
choices.outcome: You say yes on Thursday and the bishop's letter comes the next week, one paragraph. The first Wednesday at the chancery is an education in what the diocese knows about its pastors, which is more than they think and less than it should. {parish} loses an afternoon a week and does not quite notice. The younger man congratulates you at the deanery meeting and means most of it.

choices.label: Tell the vicar for clergy the younger man should have it, and say why
choices.outcome: You write two paragraphs about {@brother_priest} that you would not have written about yourself, and the bishop, who likes to be told what he was already thinking, appoints him. He calls you the night the letter comes, and is not sure what to say, and says it anyway. The deanery notices that the senior man gave something away. The chancery notices that he did not want it.

choices.label: Accept, and bring the younger man to every chancery Wednesday as your second
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy finds it irregular and allows it. For three years {@brother_priest} sits behind you at the deans' table and learns which files are read and which are signed, and when the deanery passes to him he will run it the way you did, which is the only kind of succession the Church actually has. {parish} pays for it in Wednesdays, and so do you.

choices.label: Decline. You have a parish, and the years to know what the title costs
choices.outcome: You say no and give a reason, which the vicar for clergy did not need and writes down. The deanery goes to someone else. The parish gets its Wednesday afternoons and the sick get their visits and nobody in {parish} ever knows there was a title on the table. The chancery, which keeps a list of men who say no, adds a line.

events.title: Somebody He Trusts
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} calls on a Monday and asks a favor that is not one. {@brother_priest}, a pastor twenty years your junior in the next town, is losing his school. The decision is made; the decree is drafted; the bishop will sign it after Easter. The chancery would prefer that he hear it first from somebody he trusts, over dinner, before the letter, so that when the letter comes it is already old news and he has had time to be angry somewhere private. You are the somebody. You have known him since he was a deacon at the cathedral. He has called you, twice this year, to ask whether the rumors about the school were true, and you said you had heard nothing, which was true when you said it. The vicar for clergy is not asking you to lie. He is asking you to carry a thing so that the chancery does not have to be seen carrying it, and to lend the decision your face, which after all these years is a face the younger men trust. That is the whole point, and he knows you know it.
events.flavorPrompt: The chancery uses a senior pastor as its messenger to a younger one. The register is institutional and quiet.

choices.label: Take him to dinner and tell him, the way the chancery wants it told
choices.outcome: He takes it the way a man takes it from a friend, which is worse, because he has no one to be angry at. The letter comes after Easter and is old news. The vicar for clergy thanks you in the tone that files things. You have done what the diocese does, and done it well, and the younger man will remember, later, when the school is a parking lot, who told him.

choices.label: Tell him, and tell him who sent you and what you think of it
choices.outcome: You say the chancery asked you to come and you say why, and then you say what you think of a diocese that sends a friend rather than a letter. He is angry, and then he is grateful, and the two are not in conflict. The vicar for clergy learns what you said, because the younger man repeats it, and the chancery decides you are honest and inconvenient, which it already knew.

choices.label: Tell the vicar for clergy that the bishop signs the letter and the bishop can deliver it
choices.outcome: He is quiet on the line and then says that is fair. The bishop drives out himself, which he has not done for a school closing in a decade, and the younger man gets the decision from the man who made it. The presbyterate hears, in the way it hears everything, that you refused to be the chancery's face. The chancery hears the same thing and reads it differently.

choices.label: Go to him tonight, as nobody's messenger, and tell him to get ahead of it
choices.outcome: You drive over after the evening Mass and tell him what is coming and when, and that he has a month to make the closing his own decision instead of the bishop's. He announces it himself in Lent, with a plan, and the chancery is surprised and cannot say why. The vicar for clergy suspects and cannot prove it. You have spent something you may need.

effects.value: Warned a brother priest of a chancery decision before the chancery told him

events.title: The Room Looks at You
events.body: The deanery meets in the hall of a parish that is not yours, and this month {@vicar_general} has come out from the chancery with a folder. The folder is the closing of a church in the deanery, and its pastor is {@brother_priest}, ordained eight years, who did not know until the vicar general began to speak that this was the meeting where it would be said. He is doing what a young pastor does, which is agree with the process while his hands shake. The vicar general is doing what a vicar general does, which is explain that the consultation has been completed, which is news to everyone in the room who was supposedly consulted. And the room, twelve pastors and two administrators, is doing what a deanery does when something is wrong and nobody has the standing to say so. It is looking at you. You have been in this deanery longer than anyone at the table. You have buried the man who built that church. Whatever is going to be said on behalf of the young man will be said by you or it will not be said.
events.flavorPrompt: A deanery meeting where the senior pastor must decide whether to speak for a younger one against the chancery. Procedural, tense, understated.

choices.label: Say, for the record, that the consultation did not happen and that the room knows it
choices.outcome: The vicar general writes something down. The young pastor looks at the table. The closing proceeds, six months later than it would have, with a consultation that this time actually occurs, and the parish that is losing its church gets to say so out loud, which is not nothing. The presbyterate remembers who spoke. The chancery remembers the same thing.

choices.label: Ask the procedural questions he does not know to ask: the decree, the consultation, the right of recourse
choices.outcome: You ask five questions in the voice of a man who has read the canons, and the vicar general answers four of them. The fifth, about recourse, he says he will look into. The young man learns in ten minutes what his rights are, and uses two of them. Nobody could call it opposition. The chancery calls it thorough, in the tone that means something else.

choices.label: Say nothing. A deanery is not a parliament, and the decision is made
choices.outcome: The meeting ends on time. The young pastor drives home alone and closes his church in the spring on the chancery's schedule. Two of the older men at the table find reasons not to catch your eye at the next Chrism Mass, and one of them tells you at the priests' Christmas party that he had expected more. You had expected more too. It was not the hill.

choices.label: Say nothing in the room and everything in the parking lot
choices.outcome: You catch him at his car and tell him what he should have been told: who to call at the chancery, what to ask for in writing, which canon lawyer takes clergy for nothing. He is grateful and slightly ashamed, on both your behalfs. The vicar general drives back with a clean minute. The young man gets some of what he needed, and nobody saw you give it.

events.title: The Class Is Smaller
events.body: {@closest_classmate} died in his rectory on a Tuesday, and his secretary found him on Wednesday, and by Thursday the vicar for clergy has called to say the family would like you to preach. The bishop will preside. The cathedral is being opened for it because the class, what is left of it, and the deanery, and the three parishes he served, will not fit anywhere else. You were ordained together on the same June morning with your hands on the same book. You know what he believed and what he stopped believing and what he took up again at the end. You know about the two years he nearly left, and the drinking, and the woman in the second parish, and how he came through all of it into something like peace, or at least quiet. You know that he was lonely in the way you are lonely and that he never said so to anyone but you. The bishop will say he was a faithful priest, and he was. The question is what the man who knew him says, in front of the presbyterate and the family and the bishop, about what a priest's life is actually like.

choices.label: Preach the man you knew: the loneliness, the near-leaving, and the peace at the end
choices.outcome: You say it carefully and you say all of it, and the cathedral is completely still. Three priests come to the sacristy afterward and cannot speak. The bishop shakes your hand for a moment longer than protocol and says nothing, which is a verdict of some kind. His sister thanks you for telling the truth about her brother. The chancery will not quote it. The presbyterate will.

effects.value: dead

choices.label: Preach the faithful priest the bishop will describe, and keep the rest
choices.outcome: It is a good homily and the family is comforted and the presbyterate hears what it expected. Nobody is wrong to praise it. Driving home you know that the one person who would have laughed at it is in the ground, and that you preached his funeral the way the diocese preaches every funeral, and that he would have understood and been a little disappointed.

effects.value: dead

choices.label: Preach the Resurrection and nothing else, hard and clear, the way he would have wanted
choices.outcome: Twelve minutes on the empty tomb and not a word about the man, because the man would have said that was the point. The older priests recognize what you did and why. The family is puzzled and then, a week later, consoled in a way the eulogy would not have managed. The bishop tells the vicar for clergy it was the best funeral homily he has heard in the diocese.

effects.value: dead

choices.label: Ask the bishop to preach, and sit with the family in the front pew
choices.outcome: The bishop preaches well, in general. You sit beside the sister and hold the program and do not process with the clergy, and the presbyterate notes it and does not understand it. You had nothing to say that you could say from an ambo. What you had to say you said to him on the last Tuesday, and he heard it, and that is the only homily that mattered.

effects.value: dead

events.title: Nobody Asked
events.body: The letter renewing you as pastor of {parish} arrived in the spring and you did not open it for three days, because you knew what it was. Nobody asked. The vicar for clergy's cover note says the bishop assumes you will want to stay, and the assumption is not unkind; it is what the diocese does with a man past sixty in a parish that is not on fire. It leaves him where he is, because moving him would require a decision and there is no one to move him for. Six more years. You have counted: at the end of them you will be older than the dean was when he went to the residence, and {parish} will have had you for a third of its history, and the people who remember a pastor before you will be in the cemetery you keep. There are things you could still do here. There are things you could only do somewhere smaller, or nowhere. The letter has a line for a signature and no line for anything else, and the vicar for clergy would like it back before the priests' retreat.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor's term renewed by default in his sixties. The letter is routine; what it assumes is not.

choices.label: Sign it and put it in the mail
choices.outcome: You sign it at the kitchen table. The parish never knows there was a letter, because there is always a letter. The finance council starts talking about the parking lot again as if you had never been anywhere else, and you have not, really. You are the pastor of {parish} for six more years, and the diocese has not had to think about you, and neither, this week, have you.

choices.label: Sign it, and write back asking what the diocese intends for {parish} after you
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy calls, which he does not do for signatures, and admits that there is no plan, because there is no plan for any parish, and that your asking has put {parish} on a list of places somebody should think about. That is a small thing and a real one. The chancery decides you are a man who thinks ahead, which is rare enough to be filed.

choices.label: Send it back unsigned and ask for a smaller parish for the last years
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy is surprised, and then practical: there are three small parishes waiting for anyone, and he names them. The people of {parish} hear in May that you asked to go, and some of them take it as a judgment on themselves, and the ones who know you best take it as the truth, which is that you are tired. The chancery will find something. It is not a choice, but it is smaller.

choices.label: Go and see the bishop and tell him what six more years will cost you
choices.outcome: He gives you forty minutes, which is a great deal, and listens, which is more. He does not offer a solution; he offers a second priest in residence within the year and a promise that the next letter will come with a phone call first. You sign it in his office. The diocese has heard, from your own mouth, what it is asking, and once in a while that changes something.

events.title: The Altar Steps
events.body: There are three steps up to the altar at {parish} and you have climbed them every morning for longer than some of your parishioners have been alive, and this year they have begun to climb back. It is the left knee first, at the genuflection after the consecration, a sound like a knuckle and then a moment when you are not sure it will hold. Then it is both. You have started to reach for the altar on the way down, which the servers have noticed and the people in the front pews have noticed and nobody has said. The doctor says what doctors say to men your age: it is wear, it is not going to get better, there is a surgery that works and takes six weeks, there are things you can do in the meantime. The things you can do in the meantime are all visible. A chair in the sanctuary. A rail on the steps. A bow where the rubrics ask for a knee. The older women would understand all of them. The younger men who come to the early Mass for the reverence of it would understand none of them, and one of them serves.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor's knees on the altar steps. Small, physical, and watched by the whole parish.

choices.label: Bow where you used to kneel, and say nothing about it
choices.outcome: The rubrics permit it for a priest who cannot kneel, and the parish permits it for a priest it loves, and the server at the early Mass looks at the floor the first week and then stops. The young men say nothing. One of them stops coming, and you will never know whether it was the bow. The knee is grateful in a way you do not want to admit.

choices.label: Have {@maintenance} put a rail on the steps and a chair beside the credence table
choices.outcome: The rail is brass and matches nothing and is installed on a Thursday. You use it. The chair is for after Communion and you use that too. The parish reads it correctly, as a man deciding to stay, and the Knights offer to pay for the rail, which you let them. You are visibly older in the sanctuary now and you have decided that this is not a scandal.

choices.label: The surgery, and six weeks with a walker, and a supply priest for the Masses
choices.outcome: The supply priest is a retired man who preaches long and the parish forgives him. You spend six weeks in the rectory learning what it is to be visited instead of visiting, and it is instructive. The knee is new. The parish had a pastor absent for a season and survived it, which it will remember when it needs to, and so will you.

choices.label: Kneel anyway. It is the one thing you have always done
choices.outcome: You kneel, and the knee holds, and holds, and one morning in Lent it does not, and you go down on the top step with the paten in your hand and the server catches your elbow. Nothing breaks. You finish the Mass. The parish is frightened for you in a way that is almost tender, and the doctor is not surprised, and the surgery is still there when you are ready to admit it.

effects.value: A pastor who kneels on a knee that will not hold

events.title: The Walk to the Sacristy
events.body: It is six-fifteen in January and the walk from the rectory door to the sacristy is forty feet of what the maintenance man salted last night and the wind has since undone. You have made this walk in the dark every morning of your tenure at {parish} and you make it this morning with the keys in one hand and the homily in your head, and then you are on the ground. It happens the way people say it happens: no interval. The wrist first, because you put it out, and then the hip, which is the one you are afraid of. You lie there long enough to take inventory. The wrist is wrong. The hip is bruised and not broken, you think, and you are seventy feet from anyone and the early Mass is in fifteen minutes and there are eleven people who will be in the church by then, and one of them will come looking. You can get up. That is the first thing you learn, and it is the thing that makes the next decision possible, and possibly the wrong one.
events.flavorPrompt: An old pastor falls on the ice before the early Mass. Physical, immediate, and about what he does next.

choices.label: Get up, cancel the Mass, and let {@secretary} drive you to the emergency room
choices.outcome: The wrist is broken in two places and the hip is a bruise the color of a vestment. The parish hears by noon and the casseroles begin by evening. You are out for a week and the people of {parish} discover that they can survive a week and that they do not want to. The diocese sends a card. Nobody sends a priest.

choices.label: Say the six-thirty with the wrist wrapped in a purificator, then go
choices.outcome: You say it one-handed and the eleven people know something is wrong and do not know what until you nearly drop the chalice at the ablutions. Then the emergency room, where the doctor is not amused. The parish tells the story for years: the pastor who said Mass with a broken wrist. It is a good story. The wrist heals crooked and you will feel the weather in it for the rest of your life.

effects.value: Said Mass on a broken wrist rather than cancel

choices.label: Go to the clinic quietly, tell the chancery nothing, and let the office cover the week
choices.outcome: {@secretary} runs the week with a competence that should not surprise you and does. The cast is explained as a fall on the stairs, which is nearly true. The chancery never hears, which is what you wanted, because a fall on the ice at your age is the kind of thing that starts a file. The parish suspects and lets you have it. You have hidden a thing from the diocese and it is not the first.

choices.label: Call {@brother_priest} for the week's Masses and rest as the doctor says
choices.outcome: He comes before the eight o'clock and stays the week, and says the Masses and takes the funeral and sleeps in the vicar's old room, and the parish likes him, which you note. You rest, which you have not done in a decade, and it is harder than the fall. The stipend is small. What you owe him is not, and it is the good kind of debt.

events.title: The Word
events.body: The doctor is a parishioner's son and has been your doctor for twenty years and has never, until this afternoon, closed the door of the examining room before he spoke. He says the word. He says it carefully, and then he says the other words that go with it: stage, and treatable, and schedule, and the name of a specialist in the city. He is good at this and it does not help. You drive back to {parish} and the parking lot is full because it is Wednesday and the religious education classes are letting out, and you sit in the car until it is empty. You are the pastor. The parish has a schedule and you are most of it. There is the bishop, who should be told, and the staff, who will have to cover, and the people, who will know something within a month whether or not you say it. There is treatment, which is weekly, in the city, for a season. And there is the question the doctor did not ask and could not, which is who, in a rectory with one man in it, you are going to tell first.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor's diagnosis. The register is quiet and practical; the fear is under the schedule.

choices.label: Tell the parish from the pulpit on Sunday, plainly, before the rumor does
choices.outcome: You say it after the announcements, in three sentences, and ask for prayers and for patience with the schedule. The church is silent and then it is not. By Tuesday there are meals in the rectory freezer for a month and a rota for driving you to the city. The chancery hears it from the parish before it hears it from you, which it minds a little. You have made the parish carry it, and it wanted to.

choices.label: Tell the bishop and the staff, and nobody else
choices.outcome: The bishop is kind on the phone and practical in writing: a supply priest for the treatment days, paid by the diocese. {@secretary} cries in the office and then reorganizes your calendar around the city. The parish is told you have a medical matter. It draws its own conclusions and, for a season, is gentler than usual and does not say why. You have kept it in the building, mostly.

choices.label: Tell no one, and build the schedule around the appointments
choices.outcome: The treatments are on Thursdays and Thursdays become the day you are in the city for a diocesan matter nobody can name. You say Mass on the mornings after and are grey in the sanctuary and the parish thinks you are working too hard, which is also true. You are carrying it alone because that is what you know how to do. It is heavier than the schedule shows, and the schedule shows a great deal.

effects.value: Undergoing treatment while telling no one in the parish or the diocese

choices.label: Call {@closest_classmate} from the car, before anyone
choices.outcome: He is quiet for a while and then he is himself, and he tells you what to do in the order you should do it: the bishop, the staff, the parish, and him on every Thursday in the city, which he will manage. You do it in that order. The parish carries it well. The drive to the city is the first time in years the two of you have had an hour a week, and you would not have chosen the reason.

events.title: Remission
events.body: The specialist uses the word remission the way the first doctor used the other one: carefully, with a hand on the door. The scans are clear enough. There will be scans for the rest of your life and the rest of your life is now a phrase with a shape. You drive back to {parish} on a Thursday for the first time in a season without a treatment behind you, and the parish, which has done its best, has done it visibly: the bulletin has been late four times, the finance council has met without you twice and made one decision you would not have, and the youth group has quietly stopped. The staff are tired in the way people are tired who have been holding a door. And you are a different weight than you were. You know things about the rectory at three in the morning and about being driven and about not being needed that you did not know. The schedule is on the sacristy wall in your handwriting and it is the old schedule. Nobody has told you that you have to go back to it. Nobody has told you that you can.
events.flavorPrompt: The end of treatment and the return to the parish. What the body learned; what the schedule assumes.

choices.label: Back to the full schedule by Monday, as if it had not happened
choices.outcome: By the end of the month the youth group is back and the bulletin is on time and the parish exhales, and so does the chancery. You are grey by Friday every week and say it is the weather. The body took a season to tell you something and you have told it that you were not listening. It will say it again, when it wants to, and it will not be careful about the door.

effects.value: Returned to a full pastor's schedule the week after treatment ended

choices.label: Keep the shorter week you learned in the hospital, and let the parish learn it too
choices.outcome: You take the evening meetings off the calendar and leave them off. The parish notices and a few of them mind, and the ones who drove you to the city do not mind at all. The finance council meets in the afternoon now. You are a pastor who has been sick and has said so with his schedule, and it costs something in the parish's sense of being carried, and gives something back that you had not had in thirty years.

choices.label: A Mass of thanksgiving on a Sunday, and tell them what you were told
choices.outcome: The church is fuller than Easter. You tell them the word remission and what it does and does not mean, and thank them for the meals and the driving and the patience, and the ones who did it are the ones who cry. It is the best homily you have preached in years and it is not about you, quite. The parish has been through a thing with its pastor, and it knows now what it is for.

choices.label: Ask the bishop for a month at the retreat house before you decide anything
choices.outcome: He says yes in a day and sends a supply priest, and you spend four weeks in a room with a window and the Office and a director who does not hurry you. You come back with no decision and a better silence. The parish had a fifth week without you and found it long. The chancery thinks you are fragile, which is not wrong and not the whole of it.

events.title: The Triduum You Cannot Carry
events.body: You have done Holy Week at {parish} alone before. You did it in your forties and it was a feat and you did it in your fifties and it was a week. This year you have looked at the schedule on the sacristy wall, in your own handwriting, and understood something you did not want to. The Chrism Mass is a three-hour round trip and a long standing. The Mass of the Lord's Supper has the washing of the feet, which means the floor. The Vigil is four hours if it is done right, and standing at the fire in the wind, and the Exsultet, which you have sung for thirty years and cannot now sing without your voice going somewhere in the middle. Five Masses on Easter morning. Confessions every evening. It is not that you cannot do it. It is that you know, this year, what doing it will cost the week after, and the week after that, and that you will be a worse priest through the Easter season for having been a heroic one through the Triduum. {@brother_priest} has offered to help, in the way younger men offer, which is sincerely and without knowing what it means.
events.flavorPrompt: Holy Week at the end of a career: the body sets the terms. The choice is what an old pastor gives away.

choices.label: Give {@brother_priest} the Vigil: the fire, the Exsultet, the homily, all of it
choices.outcome: He sings the Exsultet the way you did at his age and the parish hears the difference and forgives it. He preaches well. You sit in choir and receive the catechumens with him and go to bed at midnight, and on Easter morning you are a priest and not a survivor. He has done a Vigil in a parish that is not his and he will do it in his own someday and remember whose it was.

choices.label: Cut what the rubrics permit you to cut, and do the rest yourself
choices.outcome: Fewer readings, no procession, the Exsultet read rather than sung. The Triduum is done and it is done by you and it is shorter, and the families who come to {parish} for the length of it notice and say so, to each other. You are tired on Easter Monday and not broken. The parish has had a smaller Holy Week and will remember that it was smaller longer than it remembers why.

choices.label: Do all of it, alone, the way you have for thirty years
choices.outcome: You do all of it. The Exsultet goes in the middle and you finish it anyway. The five Masses on Easter morning are said and the parish is proud of you in a way that should worry it. You sleep fourteen hours on Easter Monday and cannot manage the stairs on Tuesday, and the week after Easter is said by a supply priest while you lie in the rectory listening to the bells. It was a beautiful Triduum. It was the last one you will do that way.

effects.value: A full Triduum said alone by a pastor whose body could not carry it

choices.label: Ask the deanery to cover the Triduum at {parish} between them
choices.outcome: Three pastors, each with their own Triduum, take one liturgy apiece at {parish}, because it is you asking and because they know the year is coming when it will be them. You say Easter morning and the Chrism Mass and nothing else. The parish gets three strangers in its holiest week and is polite about it. The presbyterate has done what it is for, once, and it costs you a little standing to have needed it.

events.title: Three in the Morning
events.body: You wake at three now. Not every night; most nights. The rectory at {parish} is entirely silent at three, in a way it is not at any other hour, and you lie in it and the day arranges itself in front of you in the order it will go wrong: the funeral family who are fighting, the boiler man who has not called back, the letter from the chancery you have not answered, the parishioner in the hospital who will not last the week. You have tried the things. Reading, which wakes you further. The radio, which is worse. Getting up, which means the day begins at three and you are useless by four in the afternoon, which is when the people come. The doctor has something he could give you, and has said so, and has also said, being a parishioner and an honest one, that it is not the sleep. You know what it is. It is that you have spent forty years being the man who is responsible for everything within the parish boundary, and the mind has learned to keep the watch, and it does not know that the watch could be given to someone else, because you have never tried to tell it.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor's insomnia in old age: the mind keeping a watch nobody asked it to keep.

choices.label: Get up at three and say the Office, since you are awake
choices.outcome: Matins at three in the kitchen with the light over the stove. It does not cure anything. It turns the hour into something with a shape, which is what the Office is for, and the psalms at that hour say things they do not say at seven. You are still tired by four in the afternoon. You are, at three in the morning, a priest praying, which is not nothing to be.

choices.label: Ask the doctor for the thing he has
choices.outcome: It works. You sleep until six and wake heavy and are yourself by the eight o'clock. There is a small dependence in it, which the doctor watches, and a small dullness in the mornings, which the parish does not notice and you do. The three-o'clock hour is gone and so is whatever was in it, and you have decided not to ask what that was.

choices.label: Cut the evening meetings. Nothing on the calendar after seven
choices.outcome: The parish council moves to Saturday mornings and hates it. The finance council meets at four and half of them cannot come. The rectory is yours from seven and you sleep, sometimes, until five. The people of {parish} have a pastor who is less available and more present, and they will decide over a year which of those they wanted, and it will not be unanimous.

choices.label: Tell your director that it is not the sleep
choices.outcome: He asks what you do at three and you tell him, and he asks who else could keep the watch, and you have no answer, and he says that is the answer. You do not sleep better that month. You begin, slowly, to hand things to the staff that you had never handed anyone, and the mind takes a year to believe it, and then one night you wake at five and do not know why.

events.title: The Second Glass
events.body: There has always been a drink at the end of the day. One, in the sitting room of the rectory at {parish}, with the news or without it, after the last meeting and before the Office. Every priest you respect has had the same one and most of the ones you do not. This year it is two. You did not decide that it would be two; there was a night in Lent when the first one did not do what it was for, and then a week when it did not, and then the second glass was simply where the evening went. It is not a problem. That is the sentence, and you have heard it in the confessional from men who meant it and from men who did not, and the thing you have learned in forty years of hearing it is that the sentence sounds exactly the same from both. The housekeeper has started buying the larger bottle without being asked. Nobody has said anything. Nobody would, to a pastor your age, in his own house. It is the quietest room in the building at ten o'clock and the second glass is on the table beside the chair, and you are looking at it.

choices.label: Pour it out, tonight, and tell the housekeeper not to buy it
choices.outcome: The first week is long and the evenings are longer and you say the Office at ten instead of nine because there is nothing else to fill the hour. The housekeeper does not ask. In a month the sitting room is a room again. You do not know whether it was a problem. You know that you were looking at it, and that a man who has heard that sentence for forty years knows what looking at it means.

choices.label: Tell {@closest_classmate}, who will know what it means
choices.outcome: He is quiet on the phone and then says the thing only a classmate can say, which is that he has been at two for a year and had not told anyone either. You make a rule between you, which is one, and that the other will ask. It is the smallest possible accountability and it is the only kind two old priests will accept from anyone. The second glass stays in the cabinet most nights. Not all.

choices.label: Keep it. Two is not a problem, and the rectory is quiet
choices.outcome: Two is not a problem. You are a man past sixty in a house alone with a difficult parish and forty years of other people's grief, and two is what that costs, and you have earned it. Some nights it is a large two. The eight o'clock Mass is unchanged. The parish notices nothing. You have decided that this is the shape of the evenings now, and the evenings agree with you, which is the part to watch.

effects.value: Two drinks every evening in an empty rectory, called not a problem

choices.label: You know exactly what this is. Call the number you have not called in thirty years
choices.outcome: The number still works and the man who answers is not the man who answered thirty years ago, and the meeting is in a church basement two towns over where nobody knows a pastor by sight. You go on Thursdays. You say your first name. It is the most honest hour of your week and it costs you an evening and a certain amount of pride, and you knew that when you dialed, because you have known it since you were thirty.

events.title: Three Generations
events.body: {@parishioner} calls from the hospital to say that her mother has died, and you knew before the phone rang, because you anointed her on Sunday. You buried the father twenty years ago in a snowstorm. You baptized the grandchildren, all six, and married two of them, and buried one of the marriages, and the third grandchild has not been in the church since her confirmation and will be at the funeral because it is her grandmother. The family wants what families want when a pastor has been there for all of it: they want the funeral to be about all of it. The granddaughter who does the talking would like to speak from the ambo after Communion, which the diocese discourages and you have discouraged, mostly. The son who left the Church in his thirties wants to know, through his sister, whether he can receive, and what you say will be reported to him exactly. And there is the homily, which they assume will be about her, and about them, and about you, because in this family you are not the priest. You are the man who has been there.
events.flavorPrompt: A funeral for a matriarch whose family the pastor has served for decades. The rubrics and the family's claim on him.

choices.label: The rite as written, and the family's words at the vigil the night before
choices.outcome: The granddaughter speaks at the wake, for fifteen minutes, and it is the right place for it, and she is not entirely convinced. The Mass is the Mass. You preach the readings and her name is in it four times, which is the right number. The family is grateful and a little puzzled at the restraint, and the older parishioners, who have seen you bend for others, notice that you did not bend for the ones who mattered most to you.

choices.label: Let the granddaughter speak from the ambo, and preach the family's forty years yourself
choices.outcome: She speaks for eleven minutes and cries at four of them and the church cries with her. You preach the snowstorm and the baptisms and the second marriage and the family laughs where you meant them to. It is a funeral that will be described at other funerals. It is not, strictly, the rite, and two people who know the rite write to the chancery, and the chancery, which has your file, sighs and files it.

choices.label: Take the son aside before Mass and speak to him as the man who baptized his children
choices.outcome: You find him in the parking lot and say what a priest can say to a man who has been away for thirty years, which is not the rule and not an exception to it, but an invitation to a conversation after the funeral, and you name a day. He comes. What happens after that is his. The family sees that you went to him, and it is the thing they will remember about the funeral longer than the homily.

choices.label: Preach it so well that the question of who else speaks does not arise
choices.outcome: You take the granddaughter's pages the night before, and read them, and put the best of them into a homily that is also about the Resurrection, and she hears her grandmother in it and does not ask to speak. The rite is kept. The family is given everything it wanted and did not have to take it. It costs you a night and it is the kind of thing only a man who has been there for forty years could do.

events.title: What Was Done in the Nineties
events.body: The renovation of the church at {parish} was done twenty-odd years ago, in a season of optimism, by a pastor who is now in the cemetery or by you, and either way the plaque in the vestibule has a date on it and the date is the problem. The sanctuary floor is lifting where the new tile was laid over the old without a proper bed. The sound system, which was the pride of the campaign, is a museum piece that hums. The roof over the addition was flashed by a parishioner's son who did it for cost, and the cost is now visible on the ceiling of the daily chapel in a stain the shape of a diocese. {@maintenance} has done what a maintenance man can. The architect who looked at it, a parishioner's nephew, used the word systemic, twice. You remember the campaign. You remember the pledge cards and the thermometer in the vestibule and the Sunday you said the church would be right for fifty years. It has been twenty-two. The people who gave are the people who are still here, and they remember what they were told.
events.flavorPrompt: A twenty-year-old renovation failing on the pastor who may have overseen it. Money, memory, and the next man.

choices.label: Do it properly: an engineer, a real architect, a campaign, three years
choices.outcome: You stand in the vestibule under the plaque and say that the work was not done right and that this time it will be, and the people who gave the first time give again, fewer of them and less. The engineer's report is thirty pages. The chancery approves the campaign with conditions. You will not see it finished from the pastor's chair, and you say that too, and it is the thing that makes them give.

choices.label: Patch it for what is in the account, and leave the rest to the next man
choices.outcome: The stain is painted, the tile is glued, the sound system is replaced with something from a catalogue. It looks fine from the pews. It is a problem deferred, and you know it, and the next pastor will find the engineer's report in the desk drawer where you leave it, and he will know what you knew and when. The parish is spared a campaign. The building is not spared anything.

effects.value: A failing renovation patched cosmetically and left for a successor

choices.label: Close the daily chapel and the loft, and tell the parish exactly why
choices.outcome: Daily Mass moves to the main church, which is cold and too big for eleven people. The choir sings from the floor. You explain it from the pulpit in language the engineer would recognize, and the parish, which has been told pleasant things about the building for twenty years, hears an unpleasant one and respects it more than you expected. The chancery approves of closed chapels; they are cheap.

choices.label: Bring the diocesan building office in first and make it their problem too
choices.outcome: The building office sends a man who confirms the engineer and, because the diocese now has a report with its name on it, finds a share of the money from a fund that pastors are not supposed to know exists. The campaign is smaller. The chancery has been made responsible for something, which it dislikes, and you have spent your standing there to buy the parish a roof, which is what standing is for.

events.title: Who Comes After
events.body: The parish council chair stays behind after the meeting, which he does when he has something the council should not hear first, and asks the question the parish has been asking each other in the parking lot for a year. Who comes after you. He asks it kindly. He has done the arithmetic that everyone in {parish} has done, and he wants to know whether you know, and whether you have a say, and whether the parish has one. You know more than you can tell him. You know the diocese's numbers, which are that there are not enough priests to replace the ones retiring, and that {parish} will likely be clustered with the next town, and that the man who comes will have two parishes and a vicar if he is lucky. You know that pastors do not choose successors and that the vicar for clergy will ask you anyway, informally, at the last minute. You know that the parish council chair will repeat whatever you say to twelve people by Sunday. And you know that the honest answer and the useful answer are not the same answer, and that at your age you are supposed to have learned which one to give.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish council chair asks the old pastor who will succeed him. What the diocese knows and the parish does not.

choices.label: Tell him the truth: the diocese will not replace you one-for-one, and {parish} will be clustered
choices.outcome: He is silent and then grateful, and by Sunday the parish knows, and it is angry at the diocese and not at you, which is the correct address. The chancery hears that a pastor has been describing the clustering plan in public before the chancery has, and is not pleased, and cannot say you were wrong. The parish has a year to get used to it that it would not have had.

choices.label: Say you do not know, which is true in the way that matters, and change the subject
choices.outcome: He accepts it because he has known you thirty years and because it is what he expected. The parish goes on assuming a pastor will come, and when the clustering is announced it will be a shock, and the shock will land on the man who comes and not on you. You have protected the chancery and the parish from each other for one more year, and yourself from a conversation.

choices.label: Begin bringing {@brother_priest} to {parish} on Sundays so the people know a face
choices.outcome: He says the ten-thirty once a month and preaches well enough, and the parish decides that it likes him, and the parish council chair asks whether that means what he thinks it means, and you say it means nothing, which is true. The vicar for clergy hears that a pastor is auditioning his successor and says so, mildly. When the time comes the younger man's name is already in the parish's mouth, which is worth more than a pastor's recommendation.

choices.label: Write the vicar for clergy what the parish will need, and tell the council you have
choices.outcome: The letter is three pages: the Spanish Mass that cannot be cut, the school families, the two staff who are the memory of the place. The vicar for clergy replies that it is helpful, and it is. The council chair is told that the parish's needs are on file at the chancery, which satisfies him more than it should. Nobody has been told who comes. Something has been done about it, in writing, which is what the diocese understands.

events.title: Sent to Help
events.body: The letter from the vicar for clergy says that {@brother_priest} is assigned to {parish} in residence, effective the first of the month, to assist the pastor. It does not say with what. He arrives on a Tuesday with two boxes of books and a bicycle, and by Friday he has reorganized the sacristy, proposed a young adult group, asked {@secretary} for the parish's financial statements, and used the phrase going forward in a staff meeting. He is thirty-four. He is not a bad priest. He is a priest who has been told, by someone at the chancery, that this is a parish that will need a pastor soon and that he should learn it, and he has understood that to mean that the present pastor is a man to be worked around while he is worked out. You have seen this before from the other side. You were once sent to help a man who was seventy, and you thought he was finished, and he was not, and he knew what you thought. The vicar for clergy has not called. The young man has asked, politely, when he might have the keys to the office.
events.flavorPrompt: A young priest sent in residence to an old pastor, who was once the young priest himself. The mechanics of an unspoken succession.

choices.label: Give him the school, the youth, and the Spanish Mass, and keep the rest
choices.outcome: He takes them and is good at them, and the young adult group happens, and the school families learn a new face. You keep the money, the funerals, the council, and the pulpit at the ten-thirty. He understands the division and does not like it and works within it, which tells you something you needed to know. The parish has two priests for the first time in years and prefers it.

choices.label: Give him nothing yet. Let him watch a year and learn what the parish is
choices.outcome: He says the early Masses and hears confessions and sits in on everything and runs nothing, and he is furious in the way a young man is furious, which is inwardly and on the phone to classmates. By Advent he has stopped saying going forward. By Lent he knows which families cannot be seated together. It is how you were taught. Whether it is how you should teach is a question you have decided not to ask.

choices.label: Give him the keys and step back. Say the early Mass and visit the sick
choices.outcome: You hand him the office on a Monday and he does not know what to do with it for a month and then does. The parish is confused and then adjusts, faster than you expected, which is its own lesson. You say the seven o'clock and drive to the hospital and are, for the first time since your forties, only a priest. The chancery reads it as a man preparing to go. It is not wrong.

choices.label: Call the vicar for clergy and say you did not ask for help and do not need it
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy says, in the voice of a man who has had this call before, that it is not about need. The young man stays, because assignments are not withdrawn for pride, and knows that you called, because everyone knows everything. You have made the point that you are still the pastor and you have made it to the one office that had already decided the question, and it is in the file now.

events.title: Is He Ready
events.body: The young man has been in residence at {parish} for two years and the vicar for clergy has written, which he does not usually do, to ask in a single paragraph whether {@brother_priest} is ready for a parish of his own. There is one open. The letter asks for your candid assessment and will be placed in his file, and both of you know that a file is a thing that follows a man for thirty years. He has asked you, awkwardly, in the kitchen, to say that he is. You know what he is. He is good with the school and impatient with the old and honest to a fault and a bad manager of money, and he preaches better than you did at his age and worse than he thinks. He has learned the parish. He has not learned patience, which is the thing a parish teaches and takes twenty years. You were once the subject of a letter like this, and you never learned what it said, and you have wondered for forty years which man wrote it and what he knew. The vicar for clergy would like it back within the week.
events.flavorPrompt: A senior pastor asked to assess the young priest who lived with him. What a file does to a man; what honesty costs a friend.

choices.label: Write that he is ready, and say what you would have wanted said about you
choices.outcome: Two paragraphs and generous in every line, and true in most of them. He gets the parish and calls you the night the letter comes and does not know what to say, and says it. He will make the mistakes with money that you did not warn the diocese about, and he will survive them, mostly, and he will be a pastor who knows that an old man once wrote him into a parish. That is not nothing to have done.

choices.label: Write the truth: what he does well, and what he has not learned
choices.outcome: The letter is a page and it is fair, and fair is the thing a young man cannot forgive from someone he lived with. He gets the parish anyway, with a note in the file about money that will follow him. The vicar for clergy tells you it was the most useful assessment he has read in years. The young man learns what you wrote, because they always do, and the kitchen is quiet for the last month.

choices.label: Ask that he stay one more year, for the parish's sake and for his
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy agrees, because it is easier, and the open parish goes to someone else. The young man takes it as a verdict and is right to. He stays the year and learns the patience you wanted him to learn and resents you for the whole of it, and when he leaves he is a better priest and not your friend. {parish} had two priests for a third year and was grateful, and did not know the price.

choices.label: Write it honestly, and let him read it at the kitchen table before it goes
choices.outcome: He reads it twice and is angry about one sentence and then admits the sentence is true, and you leave it in. He gets the parish. He knows exactly what his file says, which almost no priest in the diocese can claim, and he knows who told him. It is the thing you wished someone had done for you. The vicar for clergy, if he knew, would call it irregular. He does not know.

events.title: In the File
events.body: {@bishop} is making his first visit to {parish} and has brought a folder, which bishops do, and after the Mass and the lunch and the tour of the boiler he opens it in your office and takes out a photocopy. It is a page of something you said twenty years ago. A homily, or a letter to the diocesan paper, or a talk at a clergy day; you recognize the typeface before the words. He reads a sentence aloud. He reads it without expression, which is a skill, and then he asks, in the voice of a man who is genuinely curious and also keeping a record, whether you would say it now. You remember saying it. You remember the room and the reason and the man you were saying it to, who is dead. You remember that it was true and that it cost you something at the time and that you thought, at forty, the cost was paid. The file does not know that a thing can be paid for. The file knows that it was said, and by whom, and it has waited twenty years for a bishop to ask.
events.flavorPrompt: A new bishop reads the pastor's own words from twenty years ago back to him. The public record catching up.

choices.label: Say you would say it now. Then say it now
choices.outcome: You say it, and it sounds the same at sixty as it did at forty, which is either integrity or stubbornness and the bishop will decide which. He closes the folder. The visit ends on time and cordially and the chancery's regard for you moves in the direction it was always going to move. The presbyterate hears that an old man did not flinch, and the ones who agree with you are proud and the ones who do not are, privately, also proud.

choices.label: Explain precisely what it meant then and what it means now, and give him nothing to use
choices.outcome: You take fifteen minutes and you are exact: the document it responded to, the distinction it drew, the way the language has shifted since and what has not shifted underneath it. He listens like a man who did not expect a seminar. He cannot quote any of it and he knows it. The folder closes. He tells the vicar for clergy that you are a serious man, which is a category the chancery does not know what to do with.

choices.label: Say you were younger, and that you have learned
choices.outcome: It is what he wanted and he is gracious about it, and the visit ends warmly and the chancery's regard for you rises, and the file now has a second page that says the first was withdrawn. You drive to the hospital afterward and cannot remember the patient's name for a moment. The men who agreed with you twenty years ago hear what you said and understand it, and some of them will not sit with you at the next Chrism Mass.

choices.label: Say it is in the file and the file is accurate, and wait
choices.outcome: He waits too. He is good at it and you are older at it. After a while he puts the page back in the folder and asks about the school, and the visit ends as visits end. You have neither stood by it nor withdrawn it, and he will read that as he chooses. What you have not done is give him a new sentence for the file, and at your age you have learned that the file is fed by talking.

events.title: For a Piece She Is Writing
events.body: The journalist is younger than your vicar was and she is writing, she says, a long piece about {diocese} over the last thirty years: the closings, the bishops, the things that were said and the things that were done. Your name came up. It came up because of something you said in public a long time ago, which she has found in an archive and read to you over the phone in a voice that is not hostile and not warm. She would like to talk. On the record, ideally; on background if you prefer; she understands that a pastor is in a position. What she has is a quotation and a date. What she wants is the man who said it, thirty years on, saying whether the diocese has changed or he has, and what he saw, and what it cost. You know exactly what the chancery would want you to do, which is nothing, and you know that the piece will run whether you do nothing or not, and that your quotation from thirty years ago will be in it either way, with or without the sentence that comes after it.
events.flavorPrompt: A journalist finds an old public statement and asks the pastor to account for it. Press, the chancery, and a career's worth of record.

choices.label: Talk on the record, with your name on it, and say what you saw
choices.outcome: The piece runs on a Sunday and you are three paragraphs of it, accurately quoted, and the sentence that comes after the old one is there. The chancery reads it before the eight o'clock. Two brother priests call to say thank you and one to say you should have known better. You are, for a month, a man people in the city recognize in a collar, and it is not a comfortable thing to be, and you said what you saw.

choices.label: Talk on background, and let the facts carry themselves without your name
choices.outcome: The piece runs and your quotation from thirty years ago is in it, attributed, and three facts you gave her are in it, unattributed and correct. The chancery reads the facts and wonders where they came from and makes a short list. You are not on the record and you are on the list. The story is truer for what you gave it, and no one will ever know that, which you tell yourself was the point.

effects.value: Gave a journalist facts about the diocese on background

choices.label: Decline, politely. You are a pastor, not a source
choices.outcome: She thanks you and the piece runs and your quotation from thirty years ago is in it, alone, without the sentence that came after, and it reads harder than you meant it. The chancery notes that you declined, which it appreciates, and that the quotation is there anyway, which it does not. You are a man who said a thing once and would not say it twice, and that is a kind of record too.

choices.label: Call {@chancellor} first and ask what the diocese would prefer you said
choices.outcome: The chancellor is grateful for the call, which is rare, and gives you two sentences the diocese can live with, and you give them to her, and they are in the piece attributed to you and they are not untrue. The chancery has been protected by a pastor it did not think would protect it. The journalist knows what happened and writes the piece accordingly, and the reader can tell, a little.

events.title: Still a Member
events.body: {@chancellor} calls, which the chancellor does not do, and asks after the boiler, and then asks the thing he called to ask. The bishop is reviewing the presbyterate, he says, in the way new bishops do, and there is a note in your file from a long time ago about a circle you belonged to. A fraternity, a caucus, a movement; the note uses the name it had then. He wants to know, for the file, whether you are still a member. It is asked lightly. It is not light. You joined in your thirties, when it meant something to be seen with those men, and it shaped you, and some of the men are dead and some are bishops and some left the priesthood and one of them you have not spoken to in twenty years for reasons that were never about the circle. You have not been to a meeting in a decade. You have not resigned from anything. The chancellor is waiting, and whatever you say will be written down under a date, and the date will be today, and the thing you joined at thirty-five will be, in the file, a thing you affirmed or denied at your present age.
events.flavorPrompt: The chancery asks an old pastor about a circle he joined in his thirties. The register is dry; the stakes are the file.

choices.label: Say you are, and that it has not changed a homily you have preached in twenty years
choices.outcome: The chancellor writes it down. The bishop reads it, and reads the second half, and believes it or does not according to what he already thought. You have told the truth about a thing that was true at thirty-five and is true in a different way now, and you have not explained the difference, because the file has no column for it. The men who are left in the circle hear that you did not deny them.

choices.label: Say you let it lapse years ago, which is nearly true
choices.outcome: The chancellor writes it down and the bishop is reassured, and your file gains a line that closes a question. It is nearly true. The men who are left in the circle hear, because the chancery is a small building, and one of them writes to you, and the letter is short and does not accuse you of anything and you keep it in the drawer with the other letters you did not deserve.

choices.label: Say that a priest's associations are his own, and ask what the bishop actually wants to know
choices.outcome: The chancellor is silent, and then says the bishop wants to know where his priests stand, and you say the bishop can read your homilies, which are in the bulletin archive going back thirty years. It is written down as declined to answer. The presbyterate hears that an old man told the chancery to read the bulletin, and enjoys it. The bishop does not enjoy it, and will remember it at the next assignment round, if there is one.

choices.label: Tell him the history of it in {diocese}: who was in it, what it did, and what became of them
choices.outcome: It takes twenty minutes and the chancellor stops writing after five and listens, because nobody at the chancery knows this and it explains three things about the diocese that the new bishop has been puzzling over. You have named names, some of them dead and some of them not. The bishop is grateful for the map. The men still living in it are less grateful that it was drawn, and one of them hears who drew it.

events.title: Seventy-Five
events.body: You wrote the letter on your birthday, as the canon requires: a pastor who has completed his seventy-fifth year is asked to submit his resignation to the bishop, who will decide, taking all the circumstances into account, whether to accept it. You have known priests whose letters were accepted by return post and priests whose letters sat in a drawer for six years while the diocese found nobody. {@bishop} has answered. The letter is two paragraphs and kind. He accepts the resignation in principle and defers its effect; that is the phrase, and it means that you are pastor of {parish} until he says otherwise, a year at a time, and that the year could be this one. He asks, in the second paragraph, what you would like. Nobody in the diocese has asked you that in forty years. There is the parish, which does not know the letter went, and would keep you until you died in the sacristy. There is the priests' residence, and a room, and the Masses you choose to say. There is a chaplaincy somewhere with a short drive. And there is the question underneath, which is whether you are asking to stay because the parish needs you or because you do not know who you are without it.
events.flavorPrompt: The canonical resignation at seventy-five and the bishop's deferral. What an old pastor asks for when finally asked.

choices.label: Ask to stay at {parish}, a year at a time, for as long as he will have you
choices.outcome: He says yes for this year and does not promise the next, which is honest. The parish never learns that a letter went. You are a pastor on a lease, and every June is a question, and you have decided that this is preferable to the residence, which may be true and which you will find out. The vicar for clergy puts {parish} on the list of parishes with a decision pending. It was already there.

choices.label: Ask him to accept it now. Senior priest status, a room, and the Masses you choose
choices.outcome: He accepts it with a letter that thanks you for forty years in a paragraph, and the parish is told in May, and the last Sunday is full and long and the Knights give you a chair. You move to the residence in July with the books and the photographs. The parish gets a younger man in August. You say the Sunday Masses he cannot cover, at parishes that are not yours, and you are, for the first time since you were twenty-six, not responsible for a building.

effects.value: He submitted his resignation at seventy-five as the canon asks and, when the bishop offered to let him stay, asked instead that it be accepted. He left the parish in good order and in its own time, moved to the priests' residence with his books, and spent the years that followed saying the Masses younger men could not cover, in parishes that were not his, which he said was the best part of the priesthood and the part he had had least of.

choices.label: Ask for a chaplaincy, or a small parish where the Masses are few and the drive is short
choices.outcome: There is a convent with a chapel and forty sisters, most of them older than you, and a room, and one Mass a day, and confessions on Thursdays. He offers it and you take it. The parish is told, and grieves, and gets a younger man, and you are ten miles away saying Mass for women who have been praying longer than you have been alive, and it is, to your surprise, the assignment you were made for.

choices.label: Ask him, as one old man to another, what he would do
choices.outcome: He laughs, which you have not heard him do, and says that he has the same letter to write in three years and has not decided either. He tells you what he thinks, which is that a parish should not be a man's whole life and that he has never met a pastor who managed it. You stay a year. He calls in June, himself, to ask about the next one. It is the first time the two of you have been friends.

events.title: The Petition
events.body: The parish has found out. It was always going to; the secretary at the chancery is a cousin of someone, and the word resignation has been in the parking lot for a month, and now {@parishioner} has come to the office with a folder. It is a petition. It asks the bishop, respectfully, to keep the pastor of {parish} in place for as long as his health allows, and it has four hundred signatures, and there will be more by Sunday, because the Knights have it at the door. She does not ask your permission. She is telling you, because she thought you should know before the bishop does. You know what the chancery thinks of petitions. The chancery thinks a petition is a parish that has confused its pastor with its faith, and it thinks a pastor who permits one has confused himself with the parish, and it is not entirely wrong on either count. You also know that four hundred people signed a piece of paper because they do not want you to go, and that you are going, sooner or later, and that this is the only form the parish has for saying what it would otherwise say at your funeral.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish petitions the bishop to keep its old pastor. What the chancery reads into it; what it means to the man.

choices.label: Stop it. Tell her the bishop does not receive petitions about pastors, and mean it
choices.outcome: She is hurt and does what you ask, and the folder goes in a drawer with four hundred names in it that will not be read. The Knights take it off the door. The parish understands that you have chosen the diocese over them, which is not what you did, and is what it looks like. The chancery never knows there was a petition, which is the point, and you have paid for the point in the only currency the parish has.

choices.label: Let it go to the bishop, with a note of your own saying you did not ask for it
choices.outcome: The bishop receives six hundred signatures and your note, and reads the note, and believes it, mostly. He answers the parish with a letter that says nothing warmly. The chancery reads a pastor who could not control his people, and reads it into the file. You are kept for another year, which you might have been anyway. The parish believes it did that, and it is not entirely wrong, and it is prouder of you than it was.

choices.label: Tell them from the pulpit that you are tired, and that they should want a younger man
choices.outcome: It is a short homily and the church does not like it and listens anyway. You say that the parish deserves a pastor who can climb the steps, and that loving a priest is not the same as needing him, and that they will be fine, and you believe most of it. The petition stops on its own. A woman in the fourth pew says, loudly, that they will decide what they deserve. The bishop hears about the homily and is, for once, moved.

choices.label: Drive the council chair to the chancery yourself and let him say it to the vicar for clergy
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy receives a layman with a folder in the pastor's presence, which has not happened in his tenure, and hears for twenty minutes what {parish} thinks of the diocese's arithmetic. He is courteous and takes notes and promises nothing. The parish has been heard by a man with an office. You have walked a petition into the chancery, which the chancery will remember, and the parish will remember that you walked it.

events.title: The Bishop Wants the House
events.body: The vicar for clergy comes out to {parish} in person, which means it is about a building, and it is. The rectory has five bedrooms and one priest in it, and the diocese has two newly ordained men who need somewhere to live within reach of the hospital, and the bishop has looked at a map. He would like the rectory. Not immediately; the vicar for clergy uses the phrase in the coming year. You would remain pastor, for now, and the young men would be in residence, and there would be a schedule for the kitchen. Or, he says, and does not finish the sentence, because the other half of it is that a man who has resigned at seventy-five and whose resignation is deferred does not have a strong claim on a house. You have lived in this rectory longer than in any building in your life. Your books are in the room off the stairs. The people of {parish} have knocked on that door at every hour with every kind of trouble, and you have answered it, and the door is the thing they will miss when they miss you. The vicar for clergy would like to tell the bishop something by the end of the month.
events.flavorPrompt: The diocese wants the old pastor's rectory for younger men. Where a man goes when the house was the job.

choices.label: The priests' residence, and the room they have, and your books in boxes
choices.outcome: You are gone by the end of the year. The residence is quiet and the room faces a parking lot and the men at the table are your age and older and some of them are your classmates. You drive out to {parish} for the ten-thirty when the new pastor asks, which is often at first and then less. The books did not fit. It is the right thing and you did it without being told twice, and the chancery notices that too.

choices.label: Ask to stay in residence at {parish} under whoever comes, in the small room
choices.outcome: The bishop agrees, because it is cheaper than the residence, and the two young men move in and you move to the room at the end of the hall. The new pastor, when he comes, has a predecessor at breakfast. The parish keeps knocking on the door and asking for you, and you send them to him, mostly. It is a kindness to the parish and a difficulty for him and you know which one you are choosing.

effects.value: A retired pastor living in the rectory of the parish he led

choices.label: {@parishioner} has a room over the garage and has offered it, twice
choices.outcome: It is a good room and the family is kind and the arrangement is irregular in a way the chancery cannot name and does not like. You say Mass at {parish} when asked and eat with the family on Sundays and are, for the first time in your life, somebody's guest. The parish thinks it is wonderful. The vicar for clergy thinks a priest should live with priests, and says so, and you have decided he is wrong.

events.title: The Statement
events.body: The annual statement from the diocesan priests' pension plan comes in the same window envelope as the assessment, and this year you read it, which you have not done since the year it was introduced. The number is what it is. It is a number computed on forty years of a stipend that was set in a different decade by a finance council that assumed a priest would die in his rectory, and it will pay, when the bishop accepts your letter, about what a parish secretary makes, plus a room in the residence, plus the health plan, which is the thing that matters and the thing the diocese keeps quiet about because it is underfunded by a figure the presbyteral council was shown once and asked not to repeat. The collection for retired priests is in November. You have preached it every year as a duty, in three sentences, and the parish has given what it gives. You have never, in forty years, had reason to think about money for yourself. You are thinking about it. It is not a noble thing to be thinking about, and it is not nothing, and the men in the residence are not noble about it either.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor reads his own pension statement for the first time. Money in old age, quietly.

choices.label: Preach the retired priests' collection this year like you mean it, and say what it is for
choices.outcome: You say what the plan pays and what the men in the residence live on, in a homily that is not about you and that everyone understands is about you. The collection triples. Two men in the residence hear about it and write. The parish learns something about the diocese it did not know, and the chancery learns that a pastor said the number out loud, and neither is entirely comfortable with the other knowing.

choices.label: Ask the finance council to bring your stipend to the diocesan maximum, which it has never been
choices.outcome: The chair looks at the schedule and finds that you have been paid below the scale for eleven years because nobody asked, and corrects it, and does not mention it to anyone. It is a few thousand dollars and a pension calculation. It is also the first time you have asked the parish for anything for yourself, and the chair, who is kind, treats it as an oversight and not a request, which it was.

choices.label: Say nothing, and plan to keep working for as long as they will let you
choices.outcome: You put the statement in the drawer with the others. The plan is what it is and the answer is to not need it, which is the answer every priest in the residence gave, and half of them are there anyway. It is not a plan. It is a man deciding that the priesthood is what he has instead of one, which is the deal you made at twenty-six, and you have not asked to renegotiate it.

choices.label: Read the plan's actuarial report and write the finance office what is wrong with it
choices.outcome: The report is public if you know to ask and nobody has, and it takes two nights, and the letter you write is four pages and correct. The finance office is not pleased to have a pastor who can read a funding ratio. The presbyteral council asks you to present it. The plan is not fixed, because plans are not, but the number is said aloud in a room with the bishop in it, and that has not happened before.

events.title: The Will
events.body: The vicar for clergy's office sends every priest over sixty-five a form letter about wills, and every priest over sixty-five puts it in a drawer, and you have had it in the drawer for some years. This week you took it out, because a classmate died without one and the diocese and his family spent a year in a lawyer's office over a car and a savings account and four thousand books. You have more than you thought. Not much; a priest's savings are a rumor. But there is the account, and the car, and the books, and the chalice your mother bought for your ordination, and the small sum a parishioner left you in the eighties that you never spent because you did not know what it was for. The lawyer is a parishioner and will do it for nothing. He needs to know where it goes. {parish}, which will put it toward the roof and forget it. The seminary, which will put your name on a burse. Your family, who gave the Church a son and got a stipend for it. The poor, who do not write thank-you letters. It is a small thing to decide and it is the only decision you will make that you will not be present for.
events.flavorPrompt: An old priest writes his will. Small sums, and the only decision he will not see carried out.

choices.label: {parish}, all of it, for the building
choices.outcome: The lawyer draws it up in an afternoon. The chalice goes to the sacristy with a note. You tell no one, because a pastor who tells his parish he has left it money has changed what the parish is to him. It will fix a boiler someday for a pastor who never knew you, and the finance council of that year will note a bequest from the estate of a former pastor and move on to the next item, which is right.

choices.label: Your family, who gave the Church a son and got a stipend for it
choices.outcome: The nieces and nephews, in equal shares, and the chalice to whichever of them is still practicing when the time comes, which the lawyer says is not an enforceable condition and writes down anyway. You have not been much of an uncle; the priesthood does not leave room for it. This is what you have instead. It is not a great deal of money and it is a way of saying that you noticed what they gave up.

choices.label: A burse at the seminary, in your name, for a man from {diocese}
choices.outcome: The seminary's development office is very pleased and sends a brochure. The burse will pay a semester for one man every few years, and he will see your name on a list in the rector's corridor and not know who you were, and be a priest partly because of it. The chancery approves; bequests to the seminary are the kind of thing the diocese remembers a man for, and it is a good thing to be remembered for, and you are aware that you chose it partly for that.

choices.label: The books to the seminary library, the money to the poor of the parish, and nothing with your name on it
choices.outcome: The lawyer asks whether you are sure about the name and you are. The books will be shelved without a bookplate. The money will go through the St. Vincent de Paul conference, which will not know where it came from, to people who will not know either. The chalice goes to a mission. It is what you preached for forty years and it is the one time you will be held to it, and you will not be there to see whether it was worth it.

events.title: Your Brother's Keeper
