events.body: {@sibling} calls on a weeknight, which is not when family calls, and takes a long time to get to it. The house is going. There was a second mortgage that you did not know about and a business that did not work and a spouse's illness that the insurance called something else, and the bank has sent the letter that banks send, and there are eight weeks. Your sibling is not asking. Your sibling is telling you, because you are the only one left of the family who might be told, and because there is a thing everyone believes about priests, which is that they have money somewhere. You do not have money somewhere. You have a savings account that would cover perhaps a third of what the bank wants, and a pension that is not yours yet, and a rectory at {parish} with four empty bedrooms. And you have forty years of hearing, in the confessional and the office, what happens to families when the one who could help does not, and what happens to them when he does and it is not enough, and neither of those is a reason. Your sibling is waiting. The line is quiet the way a line is quiet when someone is trying not to cry.

choices.label: Give what you have. It was never going to be for anything else
choices.outcome: You wire a third of the number on Monday and it is not enough and it is the difference between eight weeks and a year, and a year is what the family needed. Your sibling does not thank you the way people thank strangers; it is quieter than that and it lasts. The savings account is what a priest's savings account should be, which is empty. You had not known you thought that until you did it.

choices.label: Tell the truth: a priest's savings are a rumor, and you are sorry
choices.outcome: You say the number you have and it is a small number and your sibling is quiet and then says it is all right, which it is not. The house goes. The family moves to something smaller near the children. The calls are shorter for a year and then they are the old length again, because it is family and family forgives the things it cannot afford not to. You told the truth and it did not help anyone and it was still the truth.

choices.label: The rectory has four empty bedrooms. Say so
choices.outcome: They come in the spring with a van and a dog and the diocese's policy on residents in rectories, which exists and which you read after they arrive. The parish is charmed and then used to it. The chancery is not charmed and sends a letter about insurance. You have a family at the kitchen table for the first time since you were a boy, and the house is louder, and it costs you an hour a day you did not have, and you would not give it back.

choices.label: Ask the parish's St. Vincent de Paul conference to help a family, and do not say whose
choices.outcome: The conference helps families every month and does not ask a pastor why. The money is small, because conference money is small, and it goes to a family two hundred miles away, which the treasurer notes and does not question. It is a gift from the poor of {parish} to a family the parish will never meet, and it is also a pastor directing parish charity to his own blood, and both of those will be true if anyone ever looks.

effects.value: Parish charity directed to the pastor's own family without disclosure

events.title: To Father, Personally
events.body: The lawyer's letter is addressed to you by name and not by office, which is the first thing you notice, and the second is the number. A parishioner you buried in the autumn, a widow with no children who came to the eight o'clock for thirty years and never asked you for anything, has left you a bequest. Not {parish}: you. The will is explicit and the lawyer, who is not a parishioner, says it was explained to her and she was clear. It is more than you have earned in any five years of your priesthood. The diocese has a policy on gifts to priests from parishioners, which you have read once and remember as discouraging and imprecise. The parish does not know. The lawyer will not tell them. The pension statement is in your drawer and you have read it. The roof at {parish} has a number too, and it is close to this one. You knew her. You know what she meant by it, which was gratitude, and you know that gratitude in the form of a check with your name on it is the kind of thing that a file, or a successor, or a journalist, reads differently than she did.
events.flavorPrompt: A widow's bequest to the pastor personally. Money, policy, and what gratitude looks like on paper.

choices.label: Sign it over to {parish}, every dollar, and tell the finance council where it came from
choices.outcome: The finance council is silent for a moment when you say the number and the name, and then the chair says the roof, and it is the roof. The bequest is entered as a gift from her estate, which is true. The parish learns, because councils talk, that the pastor was left a fortune and gave it to the building, and it does something to the way they look at you that is not entirely comfortable and is not bad.

choices.label: Keep it. The will says what it says, and the pension is what it is
choices.outcome: The check clears and goes into the account with the rumor of savings in it, and the account is, for the first time in your life, a real number. Nobody knows. The lawyer is discreet and the diocese's policy is discouraging and imprecise. You will have a room somewhere that is not the residence, if you want one. You have taken money from a parishioner and it was legal and she meant it and you will think about it at three in the morning for some years.

effects.value: Kept a large personal bequest from a parishioner without telling the parish or the diocese

choices.label: Half to the parish, half to the retirement you do not trust
choices.outcome: The parish gets a gift from her estate and does not know there was more. You get a cushion under a pension you have read. It is defensible and you have defended it to yourself in three different ways, which is more ways than a thing that is simply right requires. The roof gets half fixed. The account gets half a number. She wanted you to have it. You have decided she would have understood the arithmetic.

effects.value: Kept half of a personal bequest from a parishioner without disclosure

choices.label: Ask {@chancellor} what the diocese's policy actually requires, and do exactly that
choices.outcome: The chancellor finds the policy, which nobody has read since it was written, and it says that gifts over a threshold are to be disclosed to the bishop and that the bishop may direct them. He directs most of it to {parish} and lets you keep a sum for what the letter calls your needs in retirement. It is on file. It is the most protected money you will ever have, and the chancellor is now a man who knows something about you.

events.title: The Creed at Eight
events.body: Doubt at thirty was an argument. You remember it: the books, the professor, the night in the seminary chapel when the whole structure seemed to depend on a sentence and you could not find the sentence. It was answered, or you stopped asking, and either way you were ordained. This is not that. This is the eight o'clock Mass at {parish} on a Tuesday in February with eleven people in the pews, all of whom you have anointed or will, and the Creed comes and you say it, every word, in the voice you have used for forty years, and you notice that you are saying it the way you say the parish's phone number. Not disbelief. Something quieter. The question is not whether it is true. The question is whether anything you did with it mattered: the funerals, the boiler, the school you saved or closed, the four thousand homilies, the men you formed who left. Whether a life spent on this was a life, or a very long habit. It does not keep you up. It is there at the Creed, and at the elevation, and in the sacristy afterward when you fold the chasuble, and it has been there for a year, and you have not said so to anyone, because who would you say it to.

choices.label: Say the Creed with them. Belief is a thing you do at eight in the morning
choices.outcome: You say it the next day and the day after. It does not become an argument again and it does not become a certainty, and after a year it is what it was at twenty-six, which is a thing you do with your mouth and your knees in front of eleven people, and the doing is the belief, or is where the belief lives when it is not visiting. The eleven people never know. That is the point of the eleven people.

choices.label: Drive to your director and say it out loud, for the first time in forty years
choices.outcome: He is older than you and has heard it from older men, and says so, and does not say it is a phase, because it is not. He asks what you would do tomorrow if it were all true, and you say the eight o'clock, and he says then do that. It is not an answer. It is a man being told, at sixty, that the question is permitted, which no one told him at thirty, and the drive home is the lightest hour of the year.

choices.label: Answer it with the work. There is always more of the work
choices.outcome: You take on the second parish's confessions and the deanery's marriage cases and the hospital on Thursdays, and the question is not heard, because you are never in a room quiet enough to hear it. The parish gets a pastor who is everywhere. The question is patient. It waits in the sacristy and at the Creed and it has forty years of practice at being ignored, and it has never once gone away because it was outrun.

effects.value: A late doubt answered with more work and never spoken

choices.label: Admit that a long habit is what it was, and leave, in order and with respect
choices.outcome: You write to the bishop first and say it plainly, and he asks you to wait a year, and you wait, and it is the same at the end of the year. The parish is told in the spring and does not understand and is kind. The last Mass is full. You leave the keys on the desk and the chalice in the sacristy and you are, at sixty-odd, a man who told the truth about forty years, which is more than most men manage about one.

effects.value: He left the priesthood after forty years, having told the bishop and the parish the truth: that the Creed had become a habit and he could not go on saying it as one. He left in good order, without scandal and without a grievance, and the parish filled the church for his last Mass. He kept his friends among the clergy and most of the parish's regard, and he did not pretend to have found an answer, only to have stopped pretending he had one.

events.title: A Tuesday in Ordinary Time
events.body: It is the eight o'clock at {parish} on a Tuesday in Ordinary Time and there are nine people and the reading is one you have heard four hundred times, and at the elevation something happens that you have no word for and have not tried to find one. It is not a vision. Nothing is seen. It is that for the length of a breath the thing you have been saying for forty years is simply and entirely so, and you are inside it, and the nine people are inside it, and the boiler and the assessment and the file at the chancery are very small and very far away and also, somehow, inside it too. Then it is Tuesday again and you say the rest of the Mass. You have read enough to know what the tradition calls this and enough to distrust the naming of it, and to know that it does not come to the deserving and does not stay. In the sacristy afterward your hands are not steady and the server asks whether you are all right and you say yes, which is the first true thing you have said with that word in some time. You would like to keep it. You know that it is not the kind of thing that is kept.
events.flavorPrompt: A moment of consolation at a weekday Mass, late in a career. Restraint; no mysticism; the ordinary made briefly sufficient.

choices.label: Say the rest of the Mass, and let it be what it was
choices.outcome: You fold the chasuble and drink the coffee and answer the phone about the boiler. It does not come back that week or that year. It has changed nothing about the schedule and something about the man who keeps it, and the change is not visible to anyone, which you have come to think is the mark of the real ones. The nine people went home. One of them, you learn later, had been deciding that morning whether to come back.

choices.label: Write it down, in the notebook you have kept since seminary
choices.outcome: The notebook has four entries in forty years and this is the fifth, and it takes a page and is inadequate, and you knew it would be. You read the other four. Two of them you had forgotten entirely. That is what the notebook is for: not to keep the thing but to keep the fact that it happened, for the years when it does not, which are most of them. You put it back in the drawer with the pension statement.

choices.label: Tell {@closest_classmate} on the phone that night, badly
choices.outcome: You say it badly because there is no way to say it well, and he listens, and does not say anything about the tradition or the naming of it, and after a while says that it has happened to him twice and he has never told anyone either. You are two old men on the phone who have both been given something they did not earn and cannot describe, and it is the best conversation you have had in a decade, and it is mostly silence.

choices.label: Preach it on Sunday, without saying it was yours
choices.outcome: You preach on the elevation and what it is for, and the homily is eleven minutes and the church is unusually still, and three people say afterward that it was the best thing you have said, and you do not tell them why. It has become a homily, which is a way of giving it away, and it is a little less yours by Monday. That may be what it was for. You have not decided.

events.title: Under the Seal
events.body: There is one confession you carry. Every priest has one, and no priest says so, and you have carried yours for thirty years: a man, in a parish that was not this one, who told you in the dark what he had done to someone, and was absolved, because he asked and the conditions were met, and walked out, and you have never been able to say a word of it to anyone, and never will. That is the seal. You have kept it. You have kept it through a career in which the thing he did became the thing the whole Church was made to answer for, and you have watched other men's crimes come out and known that you hold one that did not, and could not, and the seal does not care what it costs you. He is dying now, in the hospital in the next town, and his family, who moved to {parish} some years ago and do not know that you know him, have asked for their pastor. They want you to anoint him. You have thirty years of knowing what he is and one afternoon of being his priest, and the seal, which is absolute, says nothing about whether you go.

choices.label: Go. Anoint him. You are his priest, whatever else you know
choices.outcome: He knows you when you come in. He does not say so and neither do you. You anoint him and give him viaticum and pray with the family, and drive home, and sit in the car in the rectory lot for some time. You did what a priest does and it was the hardest thing you have done in a collar and no one will ever know it was hard, which is, you have decided, the nature of the work. The seal holds. So did you.

choices.label: Send {@brother_priest}, and tell him nothing, because you can tell him nothing
choices.outcome: The younger man goes and does it well and reports that it was a peaceful death and a grateful family. You say good. You have not broken the seal and you have not gone, and the second is the thing you will think about, because the family asked for you and you sent someone else and could not say why, and they will remember that their pastor did not come. You had a reason. It is not one you can give.

choices.label: Go, and afterward tell your director only that you are carrying something you cannot name
choices.outcome: You anoint him and go home and drive the hour the next week and say to your director that there is a weight, and that it is under the seal, and that you have carried it thirty years, and nothing else. He does not ask. He says that the seal protects the penitent and not the priest, and that the Church has never found a way to carry the priest, and that he will pray for the weight without knowing its shape. It helps more than it should.

choices.label: Go, and ask him, as you would ask any dying man, whether he wishes to make his confession
choices.outcome: You ask it the way you ask every dying man, in the same words, and he looks at you for a long time and says yes, and the family leaves the room. What he says is under the seal, like the first time. What you know is that he was asked and answered, at the end, by the one priest who could not pretend not to know, and that this is what the sacrament is for, and you have never been surer of it or less comforted.
